speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to this debate with great interest. It is interesting to hear the ills of VIA Rail being compared with a medical disease, a diagnosis being prescribed and treatment being prescribed. With this in mind, I would like to offer my comments with regard to the illnesses of VIA Rail with concern for its ridership.

June 9, 1989
Supply
There is a general impression that government funding for VIA Rail is being cut at a time when the corporation's ridership figure is improving, and that VIA Rail may be turning a comer.
I will admit that ridership has indeed increased from 5.9 million passengers in 1987 to 6.4 million passengers in 1988. However, when we examine those figures more closely, we find that the 1988 ridership is only an improvement on a year-over-year basis from 1987, a year which represents the lowest ridership in VIAs history.
If one looks at the broader picture of rail passenger service in this country, one comes to the inescapable conclusion that VIA's performance has been worsening and not improving. Moreover, since its creation in 1977, VIA Rail has absorbed more than $5 billion of taxpayers' money. As we go through this debate, we have to remember that $5 billion is not a small influx of capital, as has been suggested by some speakers.
During this time the Government has made major investments in VIA to give it a fair chance to prove itself. These investments have improved service and led to savings, but never to the degree expected.
In 1987, after 10 full years of funding, the corporation experienced its lowest ever ridership level of 5.9 million passengers. A more telling comparison is between 1988 and 1981 ridership figures, since 1981 represents the year in which VIA achieved its highest ridership level of about eight million passengers. Such a comparison reveals that VIA's 1988 "improved" ridership is actually 20 per cent lower than in 1981.
The Government did make a commitment to cost-effective, modern, national passenger rail services. In doing so, however, the Government asked Canadians to share in this commitment by doing their part and take the train. This has not happened. The Government made it clear to Canadians that it would apply a "use it or lose it" approach to the funding of rail passenger services.
Since making those statements in 1984, the Government has spent more than $2.6 billion of taxpayers' money on operating and capital expenditures. That is not a small amount, as has been stated by members of the Opposition.
Despite ever-increasing subsidies, rail passenger services currently retain only 3 per cent of the total Canadian inter-city passenger traffic.
At the same time, we must remember that bus service has increased its passenger service to 6 per cent, which is double the train service; air travel has a market share of 7 per cent; and demonstrating Canadian's love affair with cars, automobiles, and trucks, those modes of transportation enjoy the lion's share of the market at 84 per cent. Those figures reveal that Canadians have a definite preference for passenger modes other than rail. They have sent a clear signal of that preference to the Government.
In light of the low-ridership levels for rail passenger services, and the Government's commitment to expenditure reduction and restraint, subsidies to VIA Rail cannot be maintained at the level the corporation is accustomed to. As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) stated: "Canadian taxpayers can no longer afford ever-increasing subsidies for a mode of transportation with decreasing ridership". By 1988, those subsidies had reached an annual level of $641 million, which translates to an average of $100 per passenger.
A member of the Opposition stated that all passenger transportation modes are subsidized. That is true. GO Transit in my area of Mississauga, Oakville, and Milton is subsidized to the tune of approximately $1.65 per passenger. Everyone can understand that. However, when the subsidy reaches $100 per passenger, something has to give.
When presented with those facts, some opponents of the Government's decision to cut subsidies to VIA Rail point to the fact that ridership performance on some services is improving. This is indeed true for the Ottawa-Toronto route where, between 1986 to 1988, traffic has increased by 29 per cent. However, the improvements made by this service have been more than offset by poor performance on other routes during the same period.
For example, ridership has declined by 15 per cent on the Victoria-Kootenay route in British Columbia, and by 26 per cent on the Moncton-Edmundston route in New Brunswick. This declining ridership is a major factor in the climb of VIA subsidies to an all-time high of $641 million. The fact remains that on a system-wide basis, seat occupancy in 1988 has been determined to be 52 per cent. In other words, for every seat occupied there is a
June 9. 1989

seat vacant. VIA must operate its services in a more-effective and rational manner.
Therefore, faced with such low performance and the prospect of ever-increasing subsidy levels, the Government made the difficult-and believe me, Mr. Speaker, it was difficult-but fiscally responsible decision to take immediate action in light of the pressing need to control the debt and the deficit.
Accordingly, a new policy approach has been adopted for VIA and new funding levels have been established for the operation of rail passenger services. I believe it is worth while reading those funding levels into the record. They are $541 million for 1989-90, $435 million for 1990-91, $394 million for 1991-92, $275 million for 1992-93, and $250 million for 1993-94. That is one-quarter of a billion dollars that will be put into rail passenger service for 1993-94.
Through these new financial limits, VIA's management is being asked to operate in a more streamlined and cost-conscious manner within a new federal Budget reality.
To achieve those objectives as soon possible, the corporation has been directed to submit a new five-year business plan that conforms to the new Budget restraints, and rises to the challenge of providing rail passenger services in a more cost-effective manner within these constraints.
There has been much discussion about truly isolated communities. In recognition of the Government's commitment to service, for truly isolated communities which have no other year-round means of transportation, the Government has asked VIA to maintain service to the truly isolated communities along VIA's remote routes in five provinces. I believe that it is worth while mentioning those routes. They are the following lines: Jasper-Prince Rupert, The Pas-Lynn Lake, Wabowden-Churchill, Winnipeg-Churchill, Winnipeg-Capreol, Sudbury-White River, Senneterre-Cochrane, Montreal-Sennet-erre, and Montreal-Jonquiere.
However, with the exception of protecting the services to isolated communities along the remote routes that I have cited, VIA's management has been given a considerable measure of flexibility in developing a new business plan. In preparing its new business plan, VIA will
Supply
consider all possible options for operating within its budget, including productivity improvements, increased fares, abandonment of routes, service reductions on some routes, and transfer of service to interested third parties. This has not been an easy thing for this Government to have to face.
Let us go back to the national debt and the deficit. One hundred per cent of Canadians recognize that we have a debt and a deficit problem in this country when 36 cents out of every tax dollar collected must go to service the debt. This is a difficult situation and the Government has taken a responsible action in putting forward a plan and asking VIA Rail to submit a new five-year plan whereby it can operate more efficiently. If only 3 per cent of Canadians want to ride the trains, why should we be asking 100 per cent of Canadians to pay $100 in subsidy for each rider of the train?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Member for Mississauga West (Mr. Horner). The current Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) stated on October 20, 1981 in regard to energy conservation:
This means that it is essential for people like the Minister of Transport to start talking trains and increased load factor, rather than

June 9, 1989

dismantling the system, but he must encourage the ever-increasing
efficiency of our rail transportation system in Canada.
In 1985, this Government under the Deputy Prime Minister who was the then Minister of Transport presented Bill C-97 to the House, an Act respecting rail passenger transportation for first reading. It never went any further. It died. Does the Member and his caucus still believe what the Deputy Prime Minister said at the time; that is, the reason why VIA Rail is not meeting its objectives is because its hands are tied, that it has not been given the opportunity to be a successful business venture because of a lack of mandate, lack of legislation and lack of commitment by the Government of the day.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I am quite sure that when the Deputy Prime Minister made those statements, he felt they could be accomplished. Believe me, we have tried. We have carried on the subsidies to the tune of $2.6 billion so that VIA Rail could act in an autonomous way.
Regarding public participation and consultation, the consultations have taken place. Canadians have said they are not interested in riding the trains. Canadians have said that only 3 per cent of us want to ride the train. Ridership is dropping throughout the country.
When I was very young there was a railway to my hometown in Pontiac County 50 miles from here. It ran from Waltham, Quebec to Ottawa. It was called the Pontiac Pacific junction but it never became the Pontiac Pacific junction because it never got across the Ottawa River and out to the Pacific. So we called it the "push, pull and jerk''-the PPJ. The "push, pull and jerk" came to Ottawa every morning and went back every night. It was a great mode of transportation for the people of that day. However, we are not in the 19th century.
In the 19th century when Sir John A. Macdonald founded the railroads, they were the only mode of travel. We did not have the highways, the automobiles or the airplanes that we have today. Canadians have made a statement that 3 per cent of them want to ride the rails. Certainly there are railroad buffs in this country. I love to see a steam train but I can see them in the museums where they should be. We are moving into the 21st century. We have to make these cuts in the interests of fiscal responsibility. We hope that VIA Rail will respond
and give the service it has to give to isolated communities in this country.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member is not implying that VIA Rail should resort to steam locomotives for transportation in this country. The Hon. Member referred to a "use it or lose it" philosophy. Does the Hon. Member feel that that "use it or lose it" philosophy should apply to other modes of transportation in this country such as the seaways, which lose millions each year and airports? I believe the only two airports in Canada that make a profit are the Toronto International Airport and the Vancouver International Airport. If he believes in the "use it or lose it" philosophy for all modes of transportation, what approach does he think this Government should take with regard to these other modes of transportation?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
As far as other modes of transportation, I know they will be subsidized. We have given a commitment and I have quoted the figures on the record of what is being given to subsidize VIA Rail to keep it going and servicing isolated communities. We will always have to subsidize certain modes of transportation.
Canadians have spoken: 84 per cent of Canadians want to travel by automobile, 7 per cent by air, 6 per cent by bus and 3 per cent by rail. If Canadians do not want to ride the trains, then why should all Canadians be forced to subsidize them to the tune of $100 for every ticket? It does not make sense. It is not fiscally responsible. Your reference to VIA Rail going back to steam trains is ludicrous. I don't believe it should, you know it and I know it.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think Members on both sides of the House agree that aside from myself, the only other Member in this House who has spoken more strongly on VIA Rail in the last number of weeks would be the Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett). We have spoken on behalf of VIA Rail for a number of reasons. The primary reason is the fact that we live in a very rural part of Canada, Atlantic Canada. We do not have the means of transportation that people in other parts of the country enjoy. Rural parts of Canada are deprived of some of the good highways and air transportation enjoyed in areas such as Ontario and Quebec and other parts of the country and larger metropolitan areas. We deserve a means of transportation that is part of our history and still serves a useful function.
June 9, 1989

We should not get lost in the numbers. There is an old expression: "Lies, damned lies and statistics". It brings home the reality of the railway. You can listen to figures until you are blue in the face, but they do not tell the real story. I am going to tell you why.
In Atlantic Canada there are only two provinces that use the railways. I believe passenger rail disappeared in Newfoundland in 1969 and does not exist in Prince Edward Island. Therefore we are talking only of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
There are approximately 1.5 million people in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I want to refer to the statistics to point out why they are sometimes misleading. Last year in Atlantic Canada, 224,000 people rode The Ocean with VIA Rail and 240,000 people rode The Atlantic. There are 500,000 people out of a population of 1.5 million who actually use that rail service. In my opinion, that 3 per cent figure is totally ridiculous. This is a figure that certainly justifies a need for that rail line in eastern Canada.
The other point I want to make, especially to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) and the Member for Mississauga West (Mr. Homer), which he addressed as well, is that in certain regions of this country we need a rail line. The subsidization that the Government pays to keep that rail line going in Atlantic Canada is lower than in any other part of the country. The Ocean is subsidized to the tune of $48.86 per passenger, and it is just over $50 for The Atlantic. The subsidy for this form of transportation in Atlantic Canada is far less than the national average.
The cost recovery percentages in relation to The Atlantic Limited indicates that it can be viable. I urge the Government to give VIA the autonomy it needs to be cost efficient and I urge it not to forget about Atlantic Canada. We do need that means of transportation. It is in our roots. It is part of our history. We don't want to lose it. We will continue to use it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to compliment my hon. friend from Atlantic Canada for those very wise remarks. Those are the issues that we have been trying to impress upon his Government over the last several weeks. I hope that he is more successful than we have been in getting that message across.
Supply
I compliment him on having the veracity to do what he just did for the benefit of all those who need rail service in our country.
Today we discussed the future of passenger rail service in Canada. The future is not promising for VIA Rail, for its workers, and the families of the workers. The future is not promising for small communities which rely on VIA Rail for their livelihoods. The future does not look promising for Canadians who rely on passenger trains for their transportation needs. The future is bleak, and unless the Government accepts the challenge that it faces and meets this problem head on, the future of passenger rail in our country is on its way out. We in the Opposition and some of those on the government side, like the Member who just spoke, must convince the Government to be bold, convince it to be imaginative in its approach, convince it to develop a philosophy and concept for the future of rail transportation in this great country of ours. If the Government does not develop this concept, I fear the loss of passenger rail service in Canada.
There can be no doubt that in developing and accepting this new philosophy, we as Canadians must accept the fact that with the exception of water traffic, moving people in Canada by rail is the least expensive way, the most energy efficient and most environmentally acceptable way throughout this great country of ours. Unless we can continue to do this, the question we must ask ourselves in this debate is not whether we can afford to keep this mode of transportation, but can we afford not to have this method of transportation for the people of Canada?
Today is not the day to look at what happened in the past, 127 years ago, with respect to railroads in Canada. Today is not the day to reiterate that the Government and the Minister who spoke earlier today said less than one year ago that insofar as rail passenger services are concerned, the Government's objective for VIA Rail is the provision of safe, modern, efficient rail passenger services across Canada.
During the last federal election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said: "The plan is for specific capital programs to enhance the quality and reliability of VIA's services. This Government is concerned about what the removal of rail service can do to a community in Canada".

June 9, 1989
Supply
Today is not the day to draw attention to the fact that the Government held public meetings throughout the country to discuss the pricing structure that could make VIA much more competitive and viable than it is today. Before the final hearing was even held on May 1, VIA's fate had been established and determined by the Budget of April 26, and the cuts that were put in place on that date.
We should not discuss today that as late as last Tuesday we were given further indications of just what the Government's direction would be with respect to the future of passenger rail service in our country. An article in The Globe and Mail outlined the intent of VIA Rail's corporate plan, a plan about which we have heard so much in the House today, which was supposed to be released at the end of this month. This five-year corporate plan calls for the elimination of 48 per cent of all VIA Rail's total operations in Canada. It includes elimination of 115 regional services throughout Canada. We also learned the plan includes the elimination of 22 routes, bearing in mind that there are only 36 routes in all of Canada. These include the elimination of four in western Canada, four in Quebec, seven in Ontario and seven routes in Atlantic Canada, unfortunately another blow to that region.
This plan cannot be denied by the Government. Paul Raynor, VIA Rail's chief of media communications, confirmed yesterday that that was the plan and the information contained in The Globe and Mail article was indeed accurate.
If this was not enough to convince Canadians of the fate of passenger rail service, the statements of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) on Tuesday provide ample evidence of the Government's vision of transportation services in our country. He said in the House that he would not give any commitments or guarantees regarding the future of VIA Rail. He then said outside the House that he would consider shutting down VIA Rail in its entirety if that is what the future for VIA Rail would be in its corporate plan.
How can the Government suggest that it is willing to give consideration to a proposal recommending the elimination of passenger rail service in our country? In good government, corporate plans are not created in a void. This corporate plan is being created in a void, without the input from all the experts on the government side and those people who work in Transport Canada.
Political direction must be given and I intend to use the balance of my time today to talk about the political motivation and where we should be going. Let us look at what the future holds for passenger rail service in Canada if we can develop a strong political leadership and develop a vision. Unfortunately, the Government does not have this vision, nor does it have the strong political leadership. The Government offers no alternatives to the position of closing out VIA Rail.
I have a very good friend, Dr. Tom Heringer, who has been a railway buff all his life. I talked to him last night about this very serious problem for Canada and he informed me that this is no longer a sentimental issue about railways in this country.
He said that if the rail system fails in our country, we will lose the link which keeps and has kept Canada together. It is a reason Canada grew from east to west, not north to south. It was one of the main reasons why Canada became a confederated nation. We stand the chance of losing the unity in Canada if we proceed on this road.
To even consider the elimination of VIA Rail shows once again complete disregard for rural and small town Canada. The small and rural municipalities which will be most severely affected by cuts to VIA Rail were not consulted by VIA Rail's master plan. The 2,500 VIA Rail employees who will lose their jobs were not consulted before this master plan took effect.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, if this shows that this Government is truly compassionate in its nature. The Conservatives will say, and naturally so, what would the Liberals do if they were faced with this problem? I say to them that this is not a Conservative problem, an NDP problem or a Liberal problem. This is a problem that faces all Canadians today.
First, let us look at what we have to build on. We have railway routes in all of Canada. We have the tracks and railbeds which are in good condition. We have railway stations. We have a competent and qualified workforce. We have the passengers who want to use the system. What is lacking is the political will, the leadership, the desire and the vision.
June 9, 1989

Let us be constructive and give the plan to this Government. For a start, I would like to say that the first thing we must do is reactivate a Bill from 1986 called Bill C-97, which gave VIA Rail the opportunity to run its own affairs, a Bill that would have unshackled the hands of VIA and let it run its own affairs like all the airlines were given in Canada.
Then we must look at our resources to provide the only thing that VIA lacks, which is modern equipment to do a good job. How could one imagine Air Canada running today if it were shackled like VIA Rail is shackled and still trying to operate the airlines in our country with DC-3 airplanes?
In Canada we have the facilities to make state of the art engines in London, Ontario. In Montreal, Kingston and Thunder Bay we have facilities to make railway cars. We have enough facilities to manufacture state of the art railway cars. In my riding, we can produce these cars.
I would like to say that if we have the will, the desire and the plan in place, we as Canadians can proceed and make VIA Rail a viable, economic railway for Canada for the next 100 years, as it was in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome that question from the Hon. Member. I thought for a while that we were talking about Canada Post today, rather than VIA Rail. If she was listening to my remarks, I did say what this country needs. If we are going to have VIA Rail continue as a viable entity within our country, it is exactly what she stated: a plan of action.
I say to her that Bill C-97, which received first reading on February 24, 1986, was a Bill designed to keep VIA Rail completely free and to unshackle its hands so that it could operate properly and would not have to go to the National Transportation Agency every time it wanted to change its salary structure or rate structure. It did not have to go to the National Transportation Agency if it wanted to change the cups that it served in its dining cars. It would have its own board of directors. It would have its own management philosophy. It would have its own methodology by which to run a viable transportation system in this country.
That Bill went nowhere, at the fault of this Government. I would suggest to the Member that that was the start of the continuing demise of VIA Rail's future in our country. Without that type of legislation, and if she will recall my speech I said that the first thing we have to do if we want VIA Rail to be viable in this country is to first accept Bill C-97 or its replacement and unshackle the hands of VIA Rail so that it can operate independently.
The second thing we have to do is take a look at the assets that VIA Rail has. I went through the good trackbeds and the stations that we have and the people in our workforce who are working for VIA Rail. There is a lot there to build on. All we have to do is go to those facilities which we already have in Canada, the railway arts in London, Ontario, which can produce state of the art engines, or to Kingston and my own plant. Can Car in Thunder Bay, which make state of the art railway cars and produce subway cars for the world. They are esteemed for their quality. The Go-Train cars, the double-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of Canadians that when we speak of transportation, this country has depended upon leaders with vision. It cried out for a government with a vision to the future and created a blueprint for the future. Instead, where do we find ourselves? We find ourselves led by an arrogant, irresponsible government with the "use it or lose it" attitude.
I would like to state from the beginning that thanks to this Government Canadians are about to lose the lifeline which weaves its way through countless small communities across this great land of ours. Canada is a country that can pull together, and pull together we did when we realized Sir John A. Macdonald's national dream. This resulted in connecting our country from east to west and from sea to sea, and is essentially the reason why we are here today.
This Government is now prepared to do away with VIA Rail at a time when it is still the primary source of transportation for thousands of Canadians. Rail transportation is no less important today than it was 100 years ago. The railway system was created not as a luxury for the people but for quite the opposite. It was seen as an inalienable right of Canadians to travel on a rail system that was theirs and would become part of their heritage. So it has become part of our heritage. However, not as the antiquated system from yesteryear, as the Government has allowed it to become, but as an extremely viable and important part of our transportation network.
For many people, train travel is a major mode of transportation for several reasons. The main reason, of course, is obvious. For those who cannot afford the costly price of an airline ticket or the cost of insuring and maintaining a family automobile, the train is the most practical and affordable way to travel. Of course, for many others airports are far too far away and if they do not have a car how are they even to get to the airport? For many communities at present, if it were not for trains living in remote or rural areas might otherwise be impossible. Travel by train is then a necessity, not a luxury.
The Government is committed to removing itself from the responsibility and duty of providing Canadians with rail service. As I have already stated, Canadians have the right to expect that the Government provide them with rail service instead of leaving them in the lurch to the dictates of the market-place where they will have to shell out large sums of money for either air or ground transportation.
Not only have Canadians been misled by the Government regarding certain commitments made in the last election, they have been misled regarding commitments made to VIA Rail. In 1987 the then Minister of Transport stated, "Over the next five years we will be spending over $2.5 billion on VIA Rail". Less than 24 months later the Government is announcing cuts to VIA Rail by hundreds of millions of dollars.
Realizing that many people rely on VIA Rail for transportation, the Government says it is too expensive to justify. In light of that reality, the Government should attempt to deal fairly with the Canadian public and VIA Rail on this very sensitive issue.
There are many things that the Government should be doing with VIA Rail but it is more concerned with abandoning it. For example, if it is the almighty buck that the Government is truly concerned about, then allow VIA Rail to set more competitive rates rather than allow the National Transportation Agency to set limits on the price of a ticket. Just as VIA Rail is due to submit a financial plan regarding the future of the corporation, the agency's chairman, former Deputy Prime Minister Erik Neilsen, has suspended hearings into VIA's pricing policy, an extremely vital process for the viability of the
June 9, 1989

corporation. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) himself concluded that the report of the hearings would form a part of a comprehensive reassessment of VIA Rail.
Not only would the loss of VIA Rail be devastating to small rural communities in terms of tourism and trade, but it would result in the loss of thousands of jobs. Mr. Tom McGrath, head of the largest union inside VIA Rail, estimates that 2,500 of VIA's 7,000 employees will lose their jobs as a result of the elimination of lines. A leaked VIA business plan obtained this week by The Globe and Mail estimated the job loss figure to be closer to 3,500.
In Moncton, New Brunswick, 1,200 jobs were lost in 1988 because CN closed its repair shops. The elimination of VIA routes would mean the city would lose another 200 jobs, plus $20 million in spin-offs. It is in small communities such as these where workers are being forced by the Government into unemployment insurance lines when they would rather be working on the railroad all the livelong day.
As well, the business plan calls for the total elimination of regional services such as routes from Toronto to Niagara Falls. Again, if such lines are not profitable, why not simply reduce the number of runs per week but keep the lines open for those who really need them instead of calling for their total eradication? In fact, the Government at the very least should have taken the lead from countries such as Britain and France and implemented high-speed trains in the major corridors.
Would it not be wonderful to hop on the train in Montreal and take it to Toronto in just two hours? Major corridor routes would be the answer for high-speed trains.
The next point I would like to address is in relation to subsidies. It is not only VIA Rail that operates with subsidies. We have heard it in speeches before this one. Airlines and bus companies have also operated on a subsidy basis. The federal Government contributes significant funds to these modes of transportation, although indirectly. For example, many buses operate on a subsidized basis because the roads on which they travel are for the major part subsidized by the Government. Each year the federal Government contributes $6 billion to road construction and repair. If VIA Rail were to be elimi-
Supply
nated, heavier usage by buses and other vehicles would dramatically and certainly increase this $6 billion figure.
Airlines receive a similar indirect subsidy. This Government not only subsidizes Canadian airlines but it allowed Boeing to purchase de Havilland at a steal. What the airlines receive is the ability to fly in and out of Canadian airports with the assistance of government-paid tarmacs, terminals, hangars, navigation and weather equipment essential to do their business.
If Canadians cannot travel by train, then what is their alternative? The Government tried to answer that question a few years back when it announced the deregulation of the Canadian airline industry. Canadians know all too well the problems with regard to air transportation under this Government. Deregulation and privatization has meant not only relinquishing what used to be the public domain, but has also meant an abdication of authority and responsibility by this Government for transportation.
In the Main Estimates for Transport Canada are included great expenditures which I am sure the Government could get around and perhaps pass on to VIA Rail. For example, at Pearson International the estimates include an additional duty-free outlet at a cost of $572,000, upgrading of floodlights at a cost of $858,000 and a long-term development study at a cost of $402,000. These three features alone total some $1.8 million.
The point I am trying to make is that while it is acceptable to preach fiscal responsibility, it is contrary to the principles of fairness that Canadians should be led to believe another thing.
I see you signalling me that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) stated that Amtrak is purchasing 100 passenger cars from Bombardier in Quebec. The catch, of course, is that the purchase is being partly financed by the Export Development Corporation, a corporation of Her Majesty. Why is it that when it comes to an American company operating the same mode of transportation the Government is thinking of phasing out in Canada, it can find Canadian taxpayers' money to finance the operation?

In closing, the strength of our national community is under siege from an arrogant, uncaring and irresponsible Government. I am concerned that 75 years of effort to build a strong, unified federal foundation is crumbling under the destructive policy actions of this Government.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Subsidies have escalated and the number of passengers has declined. This trend began in the 1950s and 1960s as travellers abandoned rail in favour of other modes of transportation. The number of passengers travelling on rail has declined by about two-thirds since a post-war high in 1947.
Each of us in this Chamber has memories of riding on the train. In 1947 my father was a Member of Parliament and I have very fond memories of taking the train with my parents to come to Ottawa to see my father speak in the House of Commons. It was a short trip. It was only
Supply
from Cobourg Station in Ontario to Ottawa, but it was a weekly trip that my father took.
When we think of memories we think of just 50 years ago, in 1939, when the late King and the Queen Mother travelled across Canada by train. The Queen Mother, of course, is commemorating that trip by returning to Ottawa on July 5 this year. There will be a very fine reception on the front lawn of Parliament Hill. I invite all Canadians to be with the Queen Mother on July 5 to commemorate the occasion of that trip of 50 years ago.
We as Canadians and as Members of Parliament share those memories of another day. Times have changed. We have to look at the present and look to the future.
In recognizing the problem as early as 1961, a royal commission on transportation recommended drastic rationalization of rail passenger services. Rationalization has been effected over time but clearly, with VIA subsidies at such alarmingly high levels, further measures are indeed needed.
This poor performance is despite expenditures of about $5 billion since VIA's creation in 1977. Of this amount, more than $1 billion went to capital investment in an effort to improve the quality and reliability of VIA's services. Of the $1 billion, more than $600 million has been spent since 1984 on major capital programs. For instance, this Government funded the purchase of 59 new high horsepower diesel locomotives for assignment to the transcontinental routes. The delivery of the first order was completed last summer and the delivery of the second order is under way. The Government also has approved the modernization of up to 100 train cars in the transcontinental fleet. These cars will receive new electric heat and air conditioning systems in order to make it more pleasant for passengers. This will restore the cars to like new conditions.
The construction of a network of equipment maintenance facilities across the country is almost completed. Facilities at Montreal and Toronto cost more than $200 million. They are state of the art in an effort to improve operational efficiency and cut the high cost of maintaining equipment.

June 9, 1989
Supply
Station and track improvements were also approved. For instance, track upgrading between Toronto and Ottawa allowed journey times to be reduced to four hours instead of the five hours that it was.
The investments that are already in place did not, however, yield lower subsidies as had been expected. The Government did its part and VIA did its best to improve the delivery of its product, but the fact is that people did not take the train. Canadians demonstrated their preference for other means of transportation. In fact, rail passenger service represents only about 3 per cent of all inter-city passenger travel in Canada.
While some have pointed to an upswing in VIA's performance in 1988 and suggest that now is not the time to cut VIA's budget, the reality is as follows. While VIA's ridership did increase by 10 per cent and revenues went up by 13 per cent in 1988, the 1988 ridership increase is being compared to 1987 when ridership plunged by 7 per cent to its lowest level ever of 5.9 million passengers. Ridership in 1988 is in fact almost identical to 1986 and 20 per cent less than was the case in 1981.
Revenues for 1988 did increase by 13 per cent, or $27 million. At the same time, operating costs increased by 15 per cent, or $94 million.
The result was the Government subsidies to VIA for its operations alone had to be increased by $68 million in 1988.
This means that for every additional dollar earned by VIA in 1988, the Government at the same time has had to disburse an additional $2.62. Clearly, the Government had to take action.
The decision to reduce the subsidy was a difficult one. It was an unavoidable one.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE

It was a very responsible one. There was the example that I just mentioned a few minutes ago. It was a very responsible action to have Canada Post put forth a business plan. At the same, time we have asked VIA Rail to put forth a business plan. We are looking forward to receiving it in the very near future.
To demonstrate its commitment to expenditure reduction and restraint and to a new regime for passenger rail service in this country, the Government has decided to
significantly reduce the subsidy it pays to VIA Rail from 1989-1990 onward.
VIA's tough but challenging budget limits are $541 million in 1989-1990; $435 million in 1990-1991; $394 million in 1991-1992; $275 million in 1992-1993; and $250 million in 1993-1994. These limits will yield savings of $500 million during the next five years.
VIA has been asked to submit a new business plan by the end of June. It is to set out the course of action with respect to the new Budget realities. In preparing its plan, VIA will consider all options to reduce its losses. Those options could include productivity, improvements, increased fares, abandonment of routes, service reductions on some routes, as well as the transfer of services to third parties.
Under any option, VIA has been directed to maintain service to truly isolated communities along nine remote routes in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. Such VIA remote area routes are Jasper-Prince Rupert; The Pas-Lynn Lake; Waboden-Churchill; Winnipeg-Churchill; Winnipeg-Capreol; Sudbury-White River; Senneterre-Cochrane; Montreal-Sennet-erre; Montreal-Jonquiere. Those are the routes that have been set out as being on truly isolated lines and should be maintained.
There have been no decisions taken yet about the future of any other VIA routes. At the same time, no options have been eliminated. The only constraints placed on VIA are to provide service to truly isolated communities along the remote routes as I have mentioned, and of course to live within its new budget.
The Government is anxiously awaiting VIA's business plan. I am sure they are working on it even today. On the basis of VIA's business plan, the Government will decide how best to proceed.
I support the Government's decision. Clearly, VIA's operations must be rationalized because of the huge burden they impose on Canadian taxpayers. The Government is acting in accordance with sound fiscal management and sound transportation policy consistent with costs and indeed consistent with usage.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes) as she eloquently tried to talk about the complete dissection and gutting of a piece of national infrastructure. If it was not so laughable, I would have been yelling across the aisle.
One of the things I find despicable in the policy of the Government is how it has intentionally misled Canadians about the future of VIA Rail. I want to remind the Member opposite that in 1985 the then Minister of Transport, currently the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) stated: "It is now time to turn VIA into a strong system that is cost effective, national in scope and one which Canadians will be proud to use".
Earlier this year the Government decided, for some strange reason, that there needed to be an inquiry into the pricing structure of VIA Rail to find out whether or not it was lessening competition with the bus lines. This was conducted, even though two or three previous investigations by the NTA had found out that the pricing structure of VIA Rail had no negative impact whatsoever on the profitability of the bus lines. Therefore, the Government set about having, I suspect, a multimillion-dollar task force to go across the country and ask Canadians: "What do you think about VIA Rail? What do you think about its pricing structure?"
I want to remind the Hon. Member opposite that the Chairman of that task force was a former Member of this House, a former Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Erik Nielsen who, in September, 1985 chaired a task force of the Hon. Member's Government.
That task force had already decided on the fate of VIA Rail. The task force stated: "Until the long-term future of its existing services is determined, postpone major capital investments in new equipment for VIA Rail other than that which is essential for transcontinental and remote services". It had already decided to have a self-fulfilling prophecy with VIA Rail. It had already decided not to invest the moneys necessary in order that Canadians could travel in comfort and on time in VIA trains.
The task force also recommended the following for cost recovery: "For the transcontinental services, a cost-recovery target of 60 per cent is to be achieved by the end of 1988 with a reduction in frequency of service where this target is not met." The decision was made long before the task force was ever set up to go about
and deceive the Canadian people and pretend that they would have some input into the decision of the Government on the future of VIA Rail.
In essence, we have a government report which suggests that the major capital investment needed to decrease the operating costs be postponed, and that an ultimatum be issued to increase revenue to 40 per cent of the cost or the federal Government was going to pull the rug out from underneath.
In the actions of the Government, what I find particularly disgusting is that it intentionally tried to tell Canadians that things were other than the way they were. It set up a task force which appeared in the Halifax-Dartmouth area. That task force was chaired by Mr. Erik Nielsen, the man who wrote the infamous document which is the death knell of VIA Rail. When the task force appeared in that area, it gave the impression that no decisions had been made.
I want to ask the Member opposite how she can justify the Government setting up this phoney task force for this sham across the country to deceive people on VIA Rail when the Government had already made its mind up to dispose of VIA Rail?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to tell Canadians what this Government has not been telling them, that the country's passenger rail service is in jeopardy and will be extinct in a short while like some animals we know. This Government has shown again that its priorities are misplaced.
We keep referring to this country's first Prime Minister because it is very important to go back into history, as the Member opposite has done, to show there was a dream. Individuals in this House are here because they have a vision and a dream of their own. His dream was to link this great land of ours from sea to sea. Surely Mr. Macdonald is turning over in his grave today with the realization that his own Party is destroying his dream of a national railway system. The railway industry has long been seen as a strong symbol of national unity. With one swing of the budget axe, Canada's strongest symbol of unity is being destroyed.
Many towns and cities were built around the railway industry. Whole communities were developed to service the thousands of workers on the rail line. Small businesses, hotels and restaurants sprung up almost overnight to cater to the needs of the railway workers. The national railway system contributed to the development of western Canada. How can this Government ignore the fact that Canada emerge as a great nation as a result of the railway industry?
Canadians learned this week that VIA Rail's corporate plan for 1989-1993 recommends that some 22 routes be eliminated, six routes will see reduced service and only six of the remote routes will be left untouched. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) says he is willing to contemplate shutting down VIA Rail's passenger service. This Government continues to ignore the fact that ridership has increased. It continues to ignore the fact that VIA Rail's profit margin has increased and that a reversing trend after two years of falling performance has begun.
It is quite clear to Canadians that this Government continues the trend of not being up front with them. Prior to the November 1988 election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised to enhance the quality and reliability of VIA Rail service. Once again
Supply
the Government has gone back on its word. Canadians know that this Government cannot be believed or trusted. What we have here, as I have said on numerous occasions in this House, is yet another broken promise.
The elimination of the transcontinental railroad between Montreal and Sudbury and Toronto-Winnipeg-Calgaiy cuts right through the heart of northern Ontario and more specifically northwestern Ontario. Many small rural and remote communities depend heavily on passenger rail service to get to major centres. Three towns in my riding will be adversely affected. The towns of Ignace, Dryden and Kenora will no longer have passenger rail service under this proposed plan. These towns will lose approximately 50 jobs as a result. The Minister may say 50 jobs is not a significant number. But 50 jobs in small town Canada is equivalent to at least 500 jobs in a major centre. How many more jobs will be lost as a result of these measures? What will the Government do to ensure that workers in the railway industry will have a job in the near future?
The Town of Ignace is a one-industry town. The Lion Lake Mine will be closing its doors soon, putting many people out of work. Now the Government is slapping this already depressed area in the face by eliminating passenger rail service. The future of the Town of Ignace is questionable. The town council is working hard at diversifying its economy but the elimination of passenger rail service through Ignace undoubtedly will hurt.
This Government is closing the door on northern Ontario. It is telling the people of northern Ontario that it is not prepared to do business, nor is it prepared to protect what is left of this region. Residents in my riding and throughout the whole northern region of Ontario now understand why the Prime Minister failed to appoint a cabinet Minister from northern Ontario. This Government is not committed to regional development.
The Minister of Transport stated recently that the federal Government is considering spending more money on highways to offset budget cuts to the passenger rail system. There is no doubt that roads in northern Ontario need upgrading. As my learned friend beside me will tell you, the Trans-Canada Highway between Winnipeg and Ottawa is in bad need of repair. It should be four-lane from at least the Manitoba border to Thunder Bay. How long will residents in northern Ontario have to wait to see their roads upgraded? Considering the record of this Government, I hate to hold my breath because I

June 9, 1989
Supply
don't believe I will be around. This is going to be another broken promise.
The Government could have chosen alternatives. Let me outline a few. VIA Rail has been paying CN and CP to support infrastructure costs of the freight rail system. In the last four years, VIA paid over $1 billion to these two railway companies. VIA has managed to reduce this figure to $100 million a year by taking over the maintenance of its own equipment. It seems to me that the Government could have introduced legislation which it did start to introduce in 1986 but it died where it was after first reading. It would have allowed CN and CP to forgive this annual payment given that the rail industry in this country is subsidized by the taxpayers. This initiative would have given VIA Rail the needed revenues to upgrade its equipment and its service.
Services have already been reduced in my riding contrary to what the Minister has been saying. The Sioux Lookout train which is in one of the most remote areas in northern Ontario has been reduced to two days a week from three days per week. Sioux Lookout is located in northwestern Ontario and serves as the focal point for many of the native communities which can only be reached by air. Many of the residents in these native communities fly to Sioux Lookout and travel by train to points south.
There are many communities in my riding which are not served by ground transportation at all. The only link to the outside world is by train. Communities such as Valora, Allan Water and many others will no longer have access to passenger rail. There are no roads linking these communities. Are they destined to be cut off from the rest of Canada? For many of the communities that have small air strips, there are no commercial flights servicing them. How can this Government justify cutting passenger rail service to these communities?
The only alternative for many residents of northern Ontario is to travel by train. Many students travelling to and from universities use passenger rail service. Many senior citizens travel by train given there is no bus service between communities in northwestern Ontario. How does the Government expect these people to get around? Many of my constituents cannot afford the luxury of flying. Furthermore, the Minister of Transport
has done nothing to alleviate their concerns over air safety in our region.
The Minister and Prime Minister are saying that Canadians are not using VIA Rail. Nothing could be further from the truth. Recently a constituent called my office to complain that he has not been able to get a reservation to head north because the trains were booked solid. Canadians are using VIA Rail. So why are they going to lose it? There is no justification for the harsh measures announced in VIA Rail's corporate plan.
The National Transportation Agency was holding public hearings across the country to review VIA Rail's pricing policy. These hearings have now stopped as a result of the Government's measures. The Government has a knack for putting the cart before the horse. It introduced legislation on a new accident investigation board before waiting for the results of the judicial review of the Gander crash and the judicial inquiry into the Dryden crash. It announced policy revisions to the Indian and Inuit Post-Secondary Assistance Program before consulting with the Indian people of Canada.
The elimination of VIA Rail's passenger service in this country is a national tragedy. The one link holding this country together from coast to coast is being dismantled piece by piece. If the Government proceeds with this plan, Canada's century old railway industry will be destroyed. Sir John A. Macdonald's vision of a national railway system will be forever lost in a fog of Tory mismanagement and unwillingness to understand what really is important to Canadians.
I suggest to Members opposite that they give this business a viable chance. There is legislation that could be put into place, and there is a legitimate opportunity for a railway system to work in Canada. But it needs the political will of the politicians to allow it to have a plan that will be effective and cost efficient.
In the last 20 years we have seen nothing of the sort. VIA has not had a chance from the beginning. We know that 60 per cent of Canadians are dead against the Government's proposal. They are in favour of trying to establish a plan for this very viable mode of transportation. If we do that, as parliamentarians, I think Canadians will accept it. They will start to use those trains if
June 9, 1989

they become reliable and efficient as they should have been many years ago.

What does a high speed line between Windsor and Quebec City mean in terms of a dedicated track, with underpasses and overpasses and so on? Where does he propose to get that money?
Of course, there are many competing demands. We need more money for research and development, for education, and for other modes of transportation. Is it the official Liberal policy that they would borrow that money and add it to the yearly deficit, therefore the national debt?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that is the official Tory line these days. It is the deficit, and to heck with the regions of Canada.
It is interesting that the Member asked the question. I might say that I am surprised that Members from western Canada have not made speeches today on behalf of their constituents because it is very important to those individuals in western Canada to have a transportation system of this nature.
The Hon. Member asked a very intelligent question concerning the source of funds. The Hon. Member should consider why VIA Rail is not cost efficient and why the subsidy is so high. First, the suggestion by the Government that it cost $600 million a year in subsidies for Canadians is not true. The fact is a little over $100 million of that money goes from one Government pocket to the next because it is a transfer for the use of track on CN alone, not to mention CP Rail. It is $100 million for the use ol that track. That is a subsidy Canadians are paying which, if removed, would only make $500 million. That is just a start.
The other problem is that VIA's hands are tied. I already stated that legislation was proposed in 1986, Bill C-97, which specifically stated a legitimate way VIA could be put into a management position where it would not have to go to the NTA to change the size of the coffee cups. It would have been able to legitimately do
Supply
business and make those business decisions to make it a viable operation.
Amtrak has done that in the United States. Its subsidies have been reduced significantly because it has been given a mandate and the ability to run on tracks without having to pay an exorbitant price to do so.
It is important that the Member first learn a little about how VIA's hands were tied and why it never got off the ground. I will admit to all Members of the House that the Liberal Party had a part to play in not putting VIA on a firm base. I might say that now we have a renewed and invigorated membership and caucus and we are looking at new ways to make this viable. We ask Members opposite to do the same and not consider deficit reduction in a vacuum.
It is very important for them to realize that if this operation is given a chance we can make it work. We are not suggesting that it can completely remove the subsidy because we would be kidding ourselves to suggest that. However, I believe that subsidy could be reduced substantially if VIA is given a chance.
The Hon. Member asks how much it would cost to make this a viable operation. Let me quote what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) said the other day concerning VIA's plans for a high-speed link. He said: "It may be kept. A $3 billion high-speed rail link between Montreal and Toronto may survive drastic cuts in the rest of Canada's rail passenger service". Out of what side of the mouth are they talking? First the Tories say there is a big deficit and we must get rid of this railway because it costs too much. How can they spend $3 billion on this one link where these individuals-and I hope I do not offend some Members from Montreal and Toronto-already have a link. They have the ability to go by air. We in the regions do not have a choice. It is either swim or walk.
I suggest that we look at the alternatives to make this operation viable. I know we can do so if there is a vision and a dream as their leader, Mr. Macdonald, had in the very early years of this great countiy of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to take part in an historical debate, for we are dealing here with much more than mere cuts to VIA Rail subsidies. We are in fact dealing with the future of passenger train service as well as the overall problem of passenger service which society will have to lace in the 21st century.
The Govemement of Canada has made its choice. It is going to sacrifice rail transportation which was the Confederation catalyst on the altar of deficit reduction. It has slashed its subsidies to VIA Rail, but has failed to provide the regions which are greatly dependant on this means of transportation with alternate solutions.
Just now, Canada is facing a crisis as far as highway and air traffic is concerned. Both are overextended, so that the safety of Canadians is being jeopardized. One needs only mention the overcrowding of Toronto's Pearson airport and the inadequate number of air traffic controllers everywhere in Canada.
Because this Government is suffering from short sightedness and obsessed with deficit reduction, our country will have to face a massive transportation crisis.
Mr. Speaker, inconsistency is the hallmark of this Government. In spite of the fact that Chairman Lawrence Hannigan claimed in VIA Rail annual report that 1988 was the best year ever in the history of that corporation, the Government has drastically reduced its assistance to VIA Rail. This cut will amount to $100 million the very first year and more than $300 million over five years.
Why is the Government scuttling VIA Rail when the corporation indicated in its annual report that the level of financing of its operations in 1988 will be 8 per cent lower for instance than in 1982, and when VIA Rail is about to achieve financial self-sufficiency?
This year, 500.000 more people used VIA Rail then last year. This 9.4 per cent increase in ridership and the 12.9 per cent increase in revenues contradict the Prime Minister's claims that Canadians don't take the train when they are travelling.
I would like to quote Mr. Hannigan in this respect:
The improvement which started last year has been sustained. The
rising trend with respect to punctuality, ridership and revenues has
been clear and constant since the fall of 1987.
And he added:
Our growth rate exceeds that for the travel market in Canada as a
whole.
Mr. Speaker, instead of helping the corporation achieve prosperity and financial independence, the present Government is destroying our national passenger rail service and wasting the public's precious tax dollars, because it will finally kill off VIA Rail if it does not maintain its contribution at a sufficiently effective level.
Taxpayers will have to pay for this Government's stubborness, but the people most directly affected will be passengers and workers. In Montreal alone, nearly 3,000 jobs are at stake. Where are the ministers from Montreal in this Government? They are nowhere. They have been gagged!
In an interview that appeared in Le Devoir, the Quebec Minister of Transport said that Ottawa's inconsistency was strangling Quebec's transportation industry.
The Minister also informed Quebecers about the federal Government's plans to abandon nearly 1,000 kilometres of railway lines in Quebec that are dedicated to freight, in addition to the decision to drop VIA Rail's regional services and reduce services in the corridors that include Montreal.
What will happen to workers in the maintenance workshops at Pointe-Saint-Charles? The decline of Quebec's railway industry also threatens 20,000 jobs in the small and medium-sized businesses that operate as subcontractors in this sector.
The schedule of cuts that appeared in the Globe and Mail indicates that the 33 lines that make up Quebec's regional transportation network will be dropped while all VIA Rail activities in the Maritimes will be shut down.
Jobs in Montreal are particularly at risk, since Pointe-Saint-Charles was the principal maintenance centre for Eastern Canada, ever since the plant we had in New Brunswick was closed.
Once again, for the sake of free enterprise, this Government is destroying, bit by bit, the very foundation of our country. In fact, the present Government has no heart, Mr. Speaker. It is reducing regional development assistance, eliminating regional railway services, and
June 9, 1989

soon the people in those regions will have to leave their homes to move to the main urban centres.
Mr. Speaker, this Government's motto is: If it doesn't make money, close it! No room for compassion. This country was built against all economic principles, but it survived and prospered because of the dedication of Canadians. Today our country is the envy of the whole world.
After the Wilson Budget, it is obvious that this Government's only law is the law of the jungle: The strongest will prevail. It is destroying our social programs one by one, is leaving Canadians to their own resources, and this philosophy also being applied to our country's remote areas. The strongest will survive and the weakest will disappear. At this rate, Canada will soon consist of Montreal, Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver, and the regions will close down one after the other, just like Schefferville.
VIA Rail is so popular among Canadians that 89 percent of them believe that it should continue giving adequate service to the people of this country. This privatization-crazed government is dismantling VIA Rail little by little and surreptitiously.
The budget speeches make clear the government's real motives. It is cutting VIA Rail's budget and asking it to rationalize its operations by increasing its fares, reducing its services and closing or selling off major components of its network. Once again, the cat is out of the bag! As in Air Canada's case, the government is abdicating its constitutional responsibility to ensure adequate transportation services for all Canadians.
According to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), if Canadians do not use VIA Rail, they will lose it. VIA Rail's annual report, which the Minister might be well advised to read, shows an increase in ridership and revenues. For the first time, this corporation is coming to the end of the tunnel and its future is looking brighter. But the Wilson budget puts a damper on this new-found vigour.
How can you possibly expect to attract more Canadians by closing down or reducing services while at the same time increasing fares?
The Government's actions leads me to the following conclusions:

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: There will be 30 seconds for the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: That will be 60 seconds, Mr. Speaker. We have just heard a litany of the same excuses provided by the Tories as the Liberals provided in 1981 and neither one of them has learned a damned thing since.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
In accordance with Standing Order 33(2)(b), it being 1.01 p.m. it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 81(14), to interrupt the proceedings and put forthwith all questions necessary to dispose of the Supply Proceedings now before the House.

The question is on the amendment. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: All those in favour of the motion will please say yea.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Yea.

June 9, 1989
Supply

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: All those opposed will please say nay.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Nay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
In my opinion the nays clearly have it.
And more than five members having risen:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 45(6), the recorded division stands deferred until six o'clock, Monday, June 12, 1989.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Although it is Friday, do you not call for the yeas and nays on both the motion and the amendment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
I must proceed with the amendment first and, once a deferred division is taken Monday night, then we will deal with the main motion depending upon the vote.
The Member for Hamilton West on a point of order.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in light of the question put to me by the Member, I am responding for the purposes of the "Blues" to clear up any misconception and to clear it up on the Member's records. Precisely what I said was that yesterday the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) stated that Amtrak is purchasing 100 cars from Bombardier in Quebec. The catch is that the purchase is, in part, being financed by the Export Development Corporation, a corporation of Her Majesty. Those are the precise words, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S. O. 81-RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: It being three minutes after three o'clock, this House stands adjourned until Monday next at 11 o'clock.
The House adjourned at 3.03 p.m.
